title: The Euthyphro dilemma
examples: Is something good because God commands it?
Can you be good without God?

explain.say: In a dialogue set in 399 BCE, the philosopher Plato shows Socrates meeting a man named Euthyphro outside a courthouse in Athens. Euthyphro is sure he knows what piety, being holy, means, so Socrates asks him a famous question.

Socrates asks: is something holy because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it is holy? Today the question is usually put about one God: is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?

draw.value: Is the holy loved by the gods because it is holy, or is it holy because it is loved by the gods?
draw.label: Socrates, in Plato's Euthyphro

explain.say: Each answer has a problem. If good just means whatever God commands, then goodness seems arbitrary; if God commanded cruelty, it would become good. If God commands things because they are already good, then goodness seems to exist apart from God.

a: Saying God is good becomes empty
draw.right: God commands it because it is good
b: God seems to follow a higher standard

explain.say: Many believers take a third path, following thinkers like Thomas Aquinas. They say goodness is part of God's own nature, so God's commands flow from that nature: they are not arbitrary, and goodness is not outside God.

items: And good does not stand outside God

draw.text: Critics ask: is God's nature good just because it is God's, or because it matches a standard? The dilemma may return.

explain.say: Muslim theologians had a similar debate. The Ash'arites held that good is what God commands, while the Mu'tazilites held that human reason can recognise good, and God commands what is good. Humanists, who are not religious, ground goodness in human wellbeing and reason.

items: God's nature: Aquinas and many believers

explain.say: So the Euthyphro dilemma is not a proof for or against God. It is a deep question about what goodness is, and believers and non-believers both use it to think more clearly about ethics.

items: Not a proof for or against God
A question about the source of goodness
Divine command, God's nature, reason, or wellbeing
Each view has strengths and critics

faq.a: The Euthyphro dilemma comes from Plato's dialogue Euthyphro, in which Socrates asks whether something is holy because the gods love it, or the gods love it because it is holy. Today it is usually put as: is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?
asks: Plato's dilemma about God and good

faq.q: Is something good because God commands it?
faq.a: That is one horn of the Euthyphro dilemma, a view called divine command theory. Supporters say God's will is the source of morality. Critics say it makes goodness seem arbitrary, since anything God commanded, even cruelty, would become good. Many believers answer that God's commands come from God's good nature.
asks: does God decide what is good

faq.a: Divine command theory is the view that what makes an action right or wrong is that God commands or forbids it. Its supporters value that it grounds morality in God. Its critics raise the Euthyphro dilemma, asking whether God's commands could then be arbitrary.
asks: what is the divine command theory of ethics

faq.a: Euthyphro is a character in Plato's dialogue, a man who meets Socrates outside the court in Athens. He is prosecuting his own father, and claims to know exactly what piety means. Socrates' questions show that defining it is much harder than Euthyphro thinks.

faq.q: What is the third option to the Euthyphro dilemma?
faq.a: Many believers, following thinkers like Thomas Aquinas, say goodness is part of God's own nature. God commands what is good because God is good, so the commands are not arbitrary, and goodness is not something outside God. Critics ask whether this just moves the dilemma to God's nature.
asks: how do believers answer the Euthyphro dilemma

faq.q: Can you be good without God?
faq.a: Many people say yes. Humanists and other non-religious people base ethics on reason, compassion and human wellbeing, and many religious thinkers agree that non-believers can know right from wrong. Some believers argue that, even so, goodness ultimately comes from God.
asks: do you need religion to be moral

faq.q: Why is the Euthyphro dilemma important?
faq.a: It asks a deep question about where goodness comes from, and it matters for everyone. If morality depends only on commands, it could seem arbitrary; if it stands on its own, then people of any faith or none might discover it by reason. Thinking it through clarifies what we mean by good.
asks: why does the Euthyphro dilemma matter

faq.q: Does the Euthyphro dilemma disprove God?
faq.a: No. It is not an argument that God does not exist. It challenges one way of explaining morality, and believers have offered several answers. It is best seen as a question about the nature of goodness.
asks: is Euthyphro an argument against God

faq.q: What did Muslim theologians say about this?
faq.a: Early Muslim theologians debated a similar question. The Ash'arites taught that actions are good because God commands them, while the Mu'tazilites taught that reason can recognise good and evil, and that God, being just, commands what is good.
Piety means being devoted and reverent towards God or the gods, doing what is holy. In Plato's dialogue Socrates asks Euthyphro to define it, and each definition Euthyphro offers runs into trouble.
Plato wrote the Euthyphro in the early 4th century BCE. It is set in 399 BCE, just before Socrates' trial in Athens, where he was condemned to death on charges including impiety.

This is the sharpest worry about divine command theory. Supporters of the God's nature reply say a perfectly good God would never command cruelty, because that would go against God's own nature. Critics ask whether that shows we judge goodness by a standard we already understand.
asks: could cruelty be good if God said so

facts: The Euthyphro dilemma comes from Plato's dialogue Euthyphro, set in 399 BCE.
Socrates asks whether the holy is loved by the gods because it is holy, or holy because it is loved by the gods.
Divine command theory holds that actions are right because God commands them.
Thomas Aquinas and many believers hold that goodness is part of God's own nature.
Muslim Ash'arite and Mu'tazilite theologians debated whether good depends on God's command or can be known by reason.

quiz.say: Recall. Which ancient philosopher wrote the dialogue in which the Euthyphro dilemma appears?
quiz.why: Plato wrote the Euthyphro, with his teacher Socrates questioning Euthyphro about piety.

wrong.1: Aristotle was Plato's student and wrote about the unmoved mover.
wrong.2: Epicurus is linked to the problem of evil.
wrong.3: Pascal lived in the 1600s and is known for his wager.

quiz.say: Apply. A student says lying is wrong only because God forbids it. Which view is this?
quiz.show: Lying is wrong only because God forbids it: which view?
quiz.why: Divine command theory holds that what makes an action wrong is that God forbids it.

wrong.1: Humanists ground right and wrong in human wellbeing and reason, not God's commands.
wrong.2: The Mu'tazilites held that reason can recognise good, and God commands it because it is good.

quiz.say: Think. Why do critics say the first horn, good because God commands it, makes morality seem arbitrary?
quiz.show: Why might good because God commands it seem arbitrary?

options.show: Anything God commanded, even cruelty, would become good
options.say: Anything God commanded, even cruelty, would become good

quiz.why: If commands alone make things good, there seems to be no reason behind them, so in principle anything could become good. Believers reply that God's good nature rules out cruel commands.

wrong.1: Many religions do teach that God gives commands; the dilemma is about what makes them good.
wrong.2: Disagreement is a different issue; the arbitrariness worry would arise even if everyone agreed.
